items.prompt: Which organ pumps blood around your body?

options.why: The lungs take oxygen from the air. They do not pump blood.
The stomach breaks down food. It does not pump blood.
The brain controls the body, but it does not pump blood.

hints: Think about which organ keeps beating all day and all night.
A pump pushes a liquid along tubes. Which organ pushes blood through blood vessels?
Press two fingers gently on your wrist. The beat you feel comes from this organ.
items.explanation: The heart is a strong muscle that squeezes many times every minute. Each squeeze pumps blood through the blood vessels to every part of the body.

items.prompt: Match each part of the body to its job.
pairs: take oxygen from the air into the blood
carry blood to every part of the body
hints: Each part has one main job. Some move blood, one takes in air and one protects.
Think about what each part is made of: a muscle, spongy bags, tubes or bones.
Find the job that needs a pump first, because only one part is a muscle that squeezes.
items.explanation: The heart pumps blood and the lungs take in oxygen. Blood vessels carry the blood, and the ribs form a bony cage that protects the heart and lungs.

items.prompt: What do veins do?

options.text: carry blood away from the heart
options.why: That is the job of arteries.

options.text: carry blood back to the heart

options.why: Pumping is the job of the heart. Veins are tubes.
Air reaches the lungs through the windpipe, not through blood vessels.

hints: There are two main kinds of blood vessel. Each kind carries blood in one direction.
Blood travels in a loop: out from the heart and then home again.
Cross out the choice that describes the heart's job, then the choice about air.
items.explanation: Veins carry blood back to the heart and arteries carry blood away from it. Together they make a loop called the circulation.
items.tip: Arteries carry blood Away from the heart: both words start with A.

items.prompt: Sort these parts into the circulatory system or the breathing system.
hints: The circulatory system moves blood. The breathing system moves air.
For each part, ask yourself whether blood or air passes through it.
Place the heart and the lungs first, then sort the tubes and the rest.
items.explanation: The heart, arteries, veins and blood make up the circulatory system. The nose, windpipe, lungs and the diaphragm muscle below them work together for breathing.

items.prompt: Wayan counts 18 beats at his wrist in 15 seconds. What is his pulse rate in beats per minute?
hints: A pulse rate tells you how many beats happen in one whole minute.
Work out how many 15-second blocks fit into one minute.
One minute is 60 seconds and 60 ÷ 15 = 4. Multiply his count by that number.
items.explanation: There are four lots of 15 seconds in a minute, so 18 × 4 = 72 beats per minute. Each beat you feel is one squeeze of the heart.

solution.say: One minute has 60 seconds. 60 divided by 15 is 4, so a minute has four 15-second blocks.
Wayan felt 18 beats in one block. Multiply by 4 to find the beats in a whole minute.
His pulse rate is 72 beats per minute.

items.prompt: The bar chart shows Citra's heart rate at rest, after walking and after running. Why is it highest after running?

figure.alt: Bar chart of Citra's heart rate: at rest 80, after walking 100 and after running 145 beats per minute.

options.text: A tired heart beats more slowly.
options.why: The chart shows the heart rate going up after running, so the heart did not slow down.

options.text: Running uses less energy than walking.
options.why: Running uses more energy than walking, so the muscles need more oxygen.

options.text: The lungs stop working while you run.
options.why: The lungs keep working. You breathe faster and deeper when you run.

options.text: Running muscles need more oxygen, so the heart pumps faster.

hints: Compare the three bars. Which activity is the hardest work for your muscles?
Muscles need oxygen and food to release energy, and blood brings both.
Ask yourself what the heart must do if the muscles need more oxygen quickly.
items.explanation: Running muscles use a lot of energy, so they need more oxygen. The heart beats faster to carry more oxygen-rich blood to them.

items.prompt: In the lungs, which gas passes from the air into the blood?

options.why: Carbon dioxide moves the other way, from the blood into the lungs, and you breathe it out.
Most of the air is nitrogen, but your body does not use it, so you breathe it back out.
You breathe out some water vapour. The gas your blood takes in is a different one.

hints: Think about which gas every cell in your body needs to release energy.
Your body takes in one gas and gets rid of a waste gas. Find each one.
Cross out the waste gas first. Then cross out the gas your body does not use.
items.explanation: Oxygen passes from the air in the lungs into the blood. At the same time, carbon dioxide passes from the blood into the lungs and is breathed out.

items.prompt: Put the parts in order to show the path oxygen takes from the air to your leg muscles.
hints: Oxygen starts in the air outside your body and ends in your leg muscles.
First follow the air into your body. Then follow the blood that picks up the oxygen.
Air goes in through your nose first. Decide which tube it goes down next.
items.explanation: Air goes through the nose and down the windpipe into the lungs, where oxygen enters the blood. The blood goes to the heart, which pumps it through arteries to the muscles.

items.prompt: How is the air you breathe out different from the air you breathe in?

options.text: It has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide.
It has no oxygen at all.
options.why: Breathed-out air still has some oxygen, just less than before.
Most breathed-out air is nitrogen. It also has some oxygen and more carbon dioxide than before.

options.text: It has more oxygen than breathed-in air.
options.why: Your body takes oxygen out of the air, so less is left.

hints: Your body keeps some gas from each breath and adds another gas to it.
Think about which gas your blood takes out and which waste gas it puts back.
Picture one breath going in and coming out. Decide which gas goes down and which goes up.
items.explanation: Your blood takes some oxygen from each breath and adds carbon dioxide. So breathed-out air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide, but it still contains some oxygen.

items.prompt: Climbers high on a mountain breathe faster, even when they are resting. Which is the best explanation?

options.text: Gravity is stronger high up, so breathing is harder.
options.why: Gravity is very slightly weaker high up, and it does not change how fast you breathe.

options.text: Cold air makes the lungs smaller.
options.why: Your lungs stay the same size. The problem is what each breath contains.

options.text: The air is warmer, so the body needs to cool down.
options.why: Air high on a mountain is colder than air lower down.

options.text: Each breath holds less oxygen, so they breathe faster to get enough.

hints: Air gets thinner the higher you go.
Think about what your body needs from each breath, and whether thin air gives enough of it.
Compare one breath at the beach with one breath on a high mountain. Decide which holds more oxygen.
items.explanation: High up, the air is thinner, so each breath contains less oxygen. The body breathes faster, and the heart beats faster, to take in and carry enough oxygen.

items.prompt: Label the organs in the chest.

figure.alt: A drawing of the chest. A tube runs down from the neck and splits to two large spongy organs, one on each side, with a smaller dark red organ between them in the lower middle.

hints: Tap a label, then tap its number.
The tube from the neck carries air down into the chest.
The two big spongy organs fill with air.
items.explanation: The windpipe carries air down to the lungs. The heart sits between the lungs and pumps blood.

items.prompt: Tap the two organs where oxygen passes from the air into the blood.

figure.alt: A drawing of the chest. A tube runs down from the neck and splits to two large spongy organs, one on each side, with a smaller dark red organ between them in the lower middle.

hints: Oxygen comes from the air you breathe in.
Think about which organs fill with air.
Look for the two organs that are the same shape.
items.explanation: Oxygen passes into the blood in the lungs. The heart only pumps the blood around.

items.prompt: Where on your body can you easily feel your pulse?

options.text: On the top of your head
options.why: The top of your head has no large blood vessel close to the skin.
A knee is mostly bone, so the pulse is hard to find there.
An ear lobe has only tiny blood vessels, so you cannot feel a beat.

hints: Your pulse is the beat of blood pushed along by the heart.
Look for a place where a large blood vessel runs close to the skin.
Doctors often press two fingers on the inside of the arm, near the hand.
items.explanation: The pulse can be felt where a large blood vessel is close to the skin, such as the wrist or the side of the neck.

items.prompt: Multiply the beats counted in 15 seconds by 4 to find the beats in 1 minute. Complete the table.
head: Activity
Beats in 15 seconds
Beats in 1 minute
hints: There are four lots of 15 seconds in one minute.
Look at the first row to see how the working goes.
Work out 24 × 4 first.
items.explanation: 24 × 4 = 96 and 36 × 4 = 144, so the pulse rate rises as the activity gets harder.

items.prompt: Amara counts her breaths for one minute during four activities. How many more breaths per minute does she take when sprinting than when sitting?

figure.alt: Bar chart of Amara's breaths per minute: sitting 16, walking 24, jogging 38, sprinting 52.

hints: Read the height of the sitting bar and the sprinting bar.
You are asked how many more, so compare the two numbers.
Subtract the smaller reading from the larger reading.
items.explanation: Sprinting is 52 breaths per minute and sitting is 16. 52 - 16 = 36 more breaths.

items.prompt: Dewi runs a race. Choose all the changes that happen in her body.

options.text: Her heart stops for a short rest.

hints: Think about what her muscles need during hard exercise.
Three of these help to get more oxygen to the muscles.
Check each choice: could the body survive it while running?
items.explanation: Working muscles need more oxygen. The heart beats faster and she breathes faster and deeper to supply it. The lungs do not shrink and the heart does not stop.

items.prompt: Blood carries oxygen to the muscles. On its way back, blood carries the waste gas called ___ to the lungs.
hints: Muscles make a waste gas when they release energy.
You breathe this gas out.
It has two words and appears in fizzy drinks.
items.explanation: Muscles make carbon dioxide as a waste gas. Blood carries it to the lungs and you breathe it out.

items.prompt: When Hadi sprints, his muscles need more ___. His heart beats ___ and he breathes ___.
hints: Think about what blood delivers to working muscles.
Hard exercise means the body must speed up its delivery.
Read each sentence aloud with each choice and see which makes sense.
items.explanation: Working muscles need more oxygen, so the heart beats faster and breathing gets deeper.

items.prompt: Tom wants to find out if jogging for longer raises pulse rate more. Which plan is a fair test?

options.text: Three different children jog for 30 s, 60 s and 90 s and compare their pulse.
options.why: Different children have different resting pulses, so you cannot tell whether time caused the change.

options.text: One child jogs for 60 s, but at a faster speed each time.
options.why: The jog stays at 60 s and only the speed changes, so this does not test jogging for longer.

options.text: The same person jogs for 30 s, 60 s and 90 s. Count the pulse for 15 s straight after each, resting in between.
One child jogs for 30 s, 60 s and 90 s but the pulse is counted at different times after stopping.
options.why: The pulse falls quickly after exercise, so the counting time must be kept the same.

hints: In a fair test you change only one thing.
Decide what to change, what to measure and what to keep the same.
Check each plan for a second thing that also changes.
items.explanation: Time jogging is the only thing changed. The same person, the same counting time and rests between tests keep the test fair.

items.prompt: Yuki counts 21 beats in 15 seconds at rest. After star jumps she counts 39 beats in 15 seconds. How many more beats per minute is her pulse after star jumps?
hints: Find the difference in 15 seconds first.
Change the difference for 15 seconds to a whole minute.
39 - 21 gives the extra beats in 15 seconds. How many 15 seconds are in a minute?
items.explanation: The extra beats in 15 seconds are 39 - 21 = 18. There are four lots of 15 seconds in a minute, so 18 × 4 = 72.

items.prompt: Sort each statement into the gas it is about.

items.text: Passes from the lungs into the blood
Needed by muscles to release energy
More of it in air you breathe in
A waste gas made by the body
Carried by the blood back to the lungs
More of it in air you breathe out

hints: One gas is used up by the body, the other is made by it.
Think about which gas you need and which you get rid of.
Start with the waste gas.
items.explanation: Oxygen goes into the blood and is used by the muscles. Carbon dioxide is the waste gas, so there is more of it in the air you breathe out.

items.prompt: The table shows Maya's pulse after she stopped running. Which sentence describes the pattern?

head: Minutes after stopping
Pulse (beats per minute)
figure.alt: Table of Maya's pulse after running: 0 minutes 150, 1 minute 122, 2 minutes 104, 3 minutes 92, 4 minutes 84, 5 minutes 78 beats per minute.

options.text: It fell quickly at first, then more slowly.
It fell by the same amount every minute.
options.why: Look at the drops: 28, 18, 12, 8, 6. They are not equal.

options.text: It stayed high for five minutes.
options.why: The pulse went down every minute.

options.text: It rose for two minutes and then fell.
options.why: The first reading is the highest one.

hints: Work out how much the pulse fell each minute.
Compare the first drop with the last drop.
The drops are 150 to 122, 122 to 104, and so on.
items.explanation: The pulse fell by 28, 18, 12, 8 and 6 beats each minute. The drops get smaller, so it fell quickly at first and then more slowly.

items.prompt: Kofi runs every day and Leo does not. Kofi's resting pulse is 58 and Leo's is 76. Which is the best explanation?

options.text: Kofi's heart is smaller, so it works more slowly.
options.why: Exercise makes the heart muscle stronger, not smaller and weaker.

options.text: Kofi's lungs make more blood at rest.
options.why: Lungs do not make blood. They take in oxygen.

options.text: Leo's heart is pumping blood to fewer places in his body.
options.why: Blood goes to every part of the body in both people.

options.text: Kofi's heart muscle is stronger, so each beat pumps more blood and fewer beats are needed.

hints: The heart is a muscle. What happens to muscles that are used often?
Think about how much blood each beat pumps.
If each beat moves more blood, how many beats are needed?
items.explanation: Regular exercise strengthens the heart muscle. A stronger heart pumps more blood with each beat, so it can beat more slowly when resting.

items.prompt: Put these steps in order to show how blood picks up oxygen and delivers it.
items: Blood with little oxygen returns to the heart in veins
The heart pumps this blood to the lungs
The blood picks up oxygen in the lungs
Oxygen-rich blood returns to the heart
The heart pumps it through arteries to the muscles
hints: The blood must collect oxygen before it can deliver it.
The heart is the pump at the start and in the middle of the journey.
Start with blood that has already been round the body.
items.explanation: Blood returns to the heart and is pumped to the lungs for oxygen. It comes back to the heart and is pumped out to the muscles.

items.prompt: Which tube carries air from your nose and mouth down to your lungs?

options.why: Arteries carry blood, not air.
Veins carry blood back to the heart, not air.
The food pipe carries food to the stomach.

hints: Air and blood travel in different tubes.
The tube you need is in your neck and is kept open by rings of strong material.
Only one of the tubes is kept open by strong rings so it never squashes shut.
items.explanation: The windpipe carries air from the nose and mouth to the lungs.

items.prompt: True or false: The heart pumps blood around the body.
hints: What does the heart do every second?
It is a muscle.
It pumps blood.
items.explanation: The heart is a strong muscle that squeezes to push blood through tubes called blood vessels to every part of the body.

items.prompt: True or false: The air that you breathe out has no oxygen in it.
hints: Does the body use all the oxygen?
You can give someone rescue breaths.
Some oxygen is left over.
items.explanation: Your body only uses part of the oxygen in each breath. Breathed out air still has about 16 per cent oxygen, plus more carbon dioxide than the air you breathed in.

items.prompt: True or false: Your heart beats faster when you exercise.
hints: What do working muscles need more of?
How does the blood get there faster?
The heart speeds up.
items.explanation: Muscles need more oxygen when they work hard, so the heart pumps faster to deliver more blood.

items.prompt: True or false: Arteries carry blood towards the heart and veins carry blood away from it.
hints: Which word starts with A for away?
Veins return blood.
Arteries go away from the heart.
items.explanation: It is the other way round. Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry blood back to it.

items.prompt: The heart pumps ___ around the body.
hints: It is red.
It carries oxygen.
It starts with b.
items.explanation: The heart pumps blood around the body.
